questions.prompt: What sets the low and high ends of a discrete amplifier's midband?
options: Coupling and bypass capacitors set the low corner; device and load capacitances set the high corner
The low corner is set by \(r_o\)
questions.explanation: Large external capacitors are shorts in the midband and open at DC; small parasitic ones are open in the midband and short at high frequency (reader Sec. 14.2).
questions.figure_alt: Amplifier gain magnitude versus log frequency: rising at low frequency below the coupling-capacitor corner, flat in the midband, falling above the high-frequency corner set by device capacitances.

questions.prompt: A source with \(R_s = 10\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\) feeds an amplifier with \(R_{in} = 100\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\) through \(C_c = 1\ \mu\mathrm{F}\). Find the low-frequency corner in Hz.
questions.explanation: The capacitor sees \(R_s + R_{in} = 110\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\): \(f_L = 1/(2\pi\cdot110\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\cdot1\ \mu\mathrm{F}) = 1.45\ \mathrm{Hz}\). Using \(R_{in}\) alone gives 1.59 Hz.

questions.prompt: Why is a capacitor placed across the source resistor of a CS stage?
options: It AC-grounds the source in the midband, restoring the undegenerated gain while \(R_S\) still stabilizes the DC bias
To block DC from the output
questions.explanation: At DC the resistor degenerates the bias; at signal frequencies the bypass shorts it.

questions.prompt: A CS stage has \(g_m = 5\ \mathrm{mS}\), \(R_D = 10\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\) and \(R_S = 1\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\) bypassed by \(C_S = 10\ \mu\mathrm{F}\) (\(r_o\) ignored). Find the frequency (Hz) where the gain is 3 dB below its midband value.
questions.explanation: \(A(s) = -g_mR_D(1 + sR_SC_S)/(1 + g_mR_S + sR_SC_S)\). The zero is at 15.9 Hz and the pole at \((1 + g_mR_S)/(2\pi R_SC_S) = 95.5\ \mathrm{Hz}\). Solving \(|A| = A_{mid}/\sqrt2\) exactly gives \(\omega R_SC_S = \sqrt{34}\), i.e. 92.8 Hz: the pole dominates.

questions.prompt: A stage has three low-frequency corners at 2 Hz, 8 Hz and 120 Hz, well separated. Roughly where is its overall low-frequency \(-3\ \mathrm{dB}\) point?
options: Near 120 Hz, the highest of the corners
questions.explanation: Coming down from the midband, the first corner you hit is the highest one. That dominant corner sets \(f_L\).
questions.figure_alt: Amplifier gain magnitude versus log frequency: rising at low frequency below the coupling-capacitor corner, flat in the midband, falling above the high-frequency corner set by device capacitances.

questions.prompt: How is the midband gain of a discrete amplifier defined?
options: With coupling and bypass capacitors shorted and device capacitances open
questions.explanation: In the midband the large capacitors are negligible impedances and the small ones are negligible admittances.
questions.figure_alt: Amplifier gain magnitude versus log frequency: rising at low frequency below the coupling-capacitor corner, flat in the midband, falling above the high-frequency corner set by device capacitances.

questions.prompt: Two buffered high-pass sections have corners at 5 Hz and 50 Hz. Find the overall \(-3\ \mathrm{dB}\) frequency (Hz).
questions.explanation: Solve \(\prod_k (f/f_k)^2/[1 + (f/f_k)^2] = 1/2\): about 51 Hz, barely above the dominant 50 Hz corner, confirming the dominant-corner rule.
questions.figure_alt: Amplifier gain magnitude versus log frequency: rising at low frequency below the coupling-capacitor corner, flat in the midband, falling above the high-frequency corner set by device capacitances.

questions.prompt: Preview of the Miller effect: what usually sets the high corner of a CS stage driven from a large source resistance?
options: \(R_s\) charging \(C_{gs}\) plus \(C_{gd}\) multiplied by the gain
questions.explanation: The input node sees the Miller-multiplied \(C_{gd}\), which often dominates.
